vignette:
She is 33 years old, Oceania, divorced, and works as a network engineer, a job she once liked for its logic and predictability. Before her son’s illness, she describes herself as someone who could always “find the fault and fix it.” When systems went down at work, she stayed calm. When life felt messy, she relied on structure, routines, and the sense that most problems could be solved if she kept her head clear.

That changed when her child becomes critically ill.

It starts with what she first assumes is a routine virus, then a fever that does not settle, then a series of appointments that begin to blur together. She remembers the moment the tone in the hospital room changes. A doctor speaks more carefully. Nurses move faster. Someone says words like “urgent,” “transfer,” and “ICU,” and she feels as if the floor has shifted under her without warning. She stands beside the bed holding her child’s small hand, watching monitors and IV lines, trying to understand everything while also trying not to panic. From that point forward, time is measured in alarms, lab results, and the rising fear that each phone call could bring worse news.

During the illness, she becomes intensely focused and almost mechanical. She tracks medications, asks questions, memorizes names, and pushes herself to stay awake through long nights. Friends tell her she is “strong,” but she experiences herself as simply unable to fall apart yet. She does not trust anyone else to notice a change quickly enough. When her child briefly improves, she cannot relax; instead, she waits for the next complication. When the child worsens again, she feels as though she is bracing for impact all the time, her body always half a second ahead of disaster.

Even after her child survives, the fear does not leave with the hospital. If anything, she says, it stays in her body. She begins to wake at small sounds in the house, convinced at first that something is wrong. Her sleep becomes shallow and broken. She dreams of hospital corridors, of being unable to reach her child, of hearing alarms she cannot stop. In the morning she is already tense, jaw tight, shoulders high, as if she has been on duty all night. She is startled by abrupt noises, by phone vibrations, by messages that light up her screen after hours. Her heart races in a way that catches her off guard, and for a moment she is back in the room where every beep seemed to matter.

She tries to return to work and discovers that concentration does not come as easily as it once did. She stares at network diagrams and loses track of what she is reading. In meetings she can hear people talking about outages, configurations, and deadlines, but part of her mind keeps drifting toward worst-case scenarios: if this system fails, then that one will fail, then everything collapses. She is still competent, but it takes more effort, and she is frustrated by how much energy it takes to appear normal. She becomes more irritable at home, especially when her child is ill with ordinary colds. Even a minor fever can send her into a spiral of scanning symptoms and checking temperatures repeatedly, unable to trust that it is nothing.

Her divorce happens after the illness, and she does not describe it as the cause so much as another loss that the trauma makes harder to bear. She feels herself becoming less available emotionally, more guarded, less able to tolerate uncertainty or closeness. She keeps people at a distance because she does not want to explain why she still cries unexpectedly, why she avoids children’s hospitals and some medical shows, why she cannot sit comfortably in a waiting room without feeling as though something terrible is about to be announced. She knows she is not “back to normal,” but she also knows she has had to keep functioning for her child, and that necessity has become part of how she survives.

In sessions, she speaks with a careful, contained style, but the fear is close to the surface. She still loves her child fiercely and is deeply protective, yet the illness has taught her that love can coexist with constant dread. She has built a life around vigilance, and even now, on ordinary days, she remains alert for the next sign that the world might once again change in an instant.
